scenario_stem:
Brackenhill Biscuits Ltd is a family-owned biscuit manufacturer in Country X that has produced shortbread and cream crackers for 11 years. Last year the business invested $480,000 in an automated wrapping and packing line using robotic arms, capable of sealing 120 packs per minute. The new equipment replaced 3 manual packing benches and 15 jobs. The owning family wants the business to stay cost-competitive against larger rivals importing cheaper biscuits.

Since the line began operating in March, output has risen from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week, and faulty seals have fallen from 4% to 1% of packs. The operations manager estimates the investment will pay for itself in under 3 years, although the 15 redundant packers received only statutory pay and morale among the remaining 60 factory workers has dipped.

questions.model_answer: Automation is the use of machines and technology to control and carry out production processes with little or no human input [2].

knowledge_max_2: Use of machines/technology to carry out tasks or control processes
Little or no human involvement or intervention in the process

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackenhill Biscuits of automating its packing line.
questions.model_answer: First, the line raised productivity [k], sealing 120 packs per minute and lifting weekly output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs [app]. Second, product quality improved [k], as faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher productivity/output per period
Improved and more consistent product quality or fewer errors
application_max_2: Line seals 120 packs per minute and weekly output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs
Faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Brackenhill Biscuits of introducing the automated line.
questions.model_answer: First, redundancies [k]: the business made 15 packers redundant, so they received only statutory pay [app], and lower morale among the remaining 60 factory workers could raise absenteeism and errors [an]. Second, high capital outlay [k]: $480,000 had to be spent before the estimated payback of under 3 years [app], so if weekly output falls short of 52,000 packs the family may struggle to recover the cost and stay competitive against imports [an].

knowledge_max_2: Redundancies and loss of jobs
High initial capital cost of the investment
application_max_2: 15 packers made redundant and paid only statutory pay; morale dipped among the remaining 60 factory workers
$480,000 was invested with payback estimated at under 3 years
analysis_max_2: Poorer morale could increase absenteeism and mistakes on the line

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenhill Biscuits should invest in automated mixing and baking equipment as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, further automation should raise productivity [k]; the packing line lifted output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week and cut faulty seals from 4% to 1% [app]; extending the same technology to mixing and baking could remove more errors, lower unit costs and keep biscuits cheaper than imports [an]. However, automation destroyed jobs [k]; this project cost $480,000, made the 15 redundant packers leave on statutory pay and soured morale among the remaining 60 factory workers [app]; repeating that scale of disruption in mixing and baking, where timing and temperature need judgement, could deepen absenteeism and hurt consistency [an]. Overall I recommend phased investment in automated mixing first, with skilled staff retrained and supervising [eval]; baking should keep human oversight for now, so automating both stages fully would be premature given the morale damage already seen [eval].

Automation causes redundancies, high capital cost and morale problems

scenario_stem:
Cinderford Brickworks is a brick manufacturer in Country X that has supplied builders for 14 years, producing facing and engineering bricks for housebuilders across the region. Two years ago the owners spent $250,000 installing a mechanised extrusion machine and automatic wire-cutter, allowing operators to feed clay rather than mould bricks by hand. The yard now employs 74 workers, 30 of whom run the machines.

Output has risen from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week, and reject bricks have fallen from 7% to 3%. Hourly wages of $11.50 for machine operators tempt the business to recruit 6 more workers this year, but clay prices have climbed 12%. The kilns are now the production bottleneck, and the owners have delayed a planned wage rise until 2027 while they repay the machine loan.

questions.model_answer: Mechanisation is the use of machines to carry out work that was previously done by hand, with workers still operating or controlling the machines [2].

knowledge_max_2: Use of machines to replace or assist manual labour
Human operators still control or supervise the machines

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Cinderford Brickworks introduced mechanised machines.
questions.model_answer: First, to raise output [k]; the mechanised extruder and wire-cutter lifted production from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week [app]. Second, to cut waste [k]; reject bricks fell from 7% to 3% after the machines were installed [app].

knowledge_max_2: To increase output/productivity
To reduce waste, rejects and human error
application_max_2: Production rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week
Reject bricks fell from 7% to 3%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Cinderford Brickworks may face from its mechanisation.
questions.model_answer: First, dependence on skilled operators [k]: the business relies on 30 of its 74 workers to run the machines at $11.50 per hour [app], so any absence or breakdown could stop extrusion and widen the kiln bottleneck [an]. Second, rising input costs [k]: clay prices have climbed 12% [app], squeezing margins and making it harder to recover the $250,000 outlay without raising brick prices for builders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on specialist operators and machine breakdowns
Higher costs or repayment burden after investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Cinderford Brickworks should now invest in mechanising the kilns as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, mechanising the kilns would attack the bottleneck [k]; the yard already lifted output from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week and cut rejects from 7% to 3% by mechanising extrusion [app]; applying the same approach to firing could raise capacity and stabilise quality while builder demand keeps growing [an]. However, machines reduce rather than increase labour needs [k]; the business has already spent $250,000 and pays operators $11.50 per hour amid a 12% clay price rise [app], and another large outlay plus recruiting 6 more workers risks overstretching cash if the housing market slows [an]. Overall I recommend phased kiln mechanisation funded largely from retained profit, because the proven 50% output gain outweighs the cost risk, provided the new recruits are trained to operate the machines before phase two begins [eval]; if clay costs keep climbing, phase two should be delayed rather than debt-financed [eval].

scenario_stem:
Halyard Lighting Co is a manufacturer of decorative ceiling lamps, wall lights and brass fittings in Country X, trading for 9 years. Its design team of 6 uses CAD software that cost $95,000 to create and modify lamp designs on screen before any prototype is built. Design revisions that once took 3 weeks can now be completed in 4 days.

Sales last year reached $2.1 million. Prototyping waste fell by 40%, but the finance director warns the software licence is due for renewal at $18,000 per year and two senior designers were hired on $42,000 salaries to run it. The board values the design edge CAD gives against copycat rivals, yet must now decide whether to buy 2 more CAD licences or hire another designer.

questions.model_answer: CAD is the use of computer software to create, modify and test product designs digitally before any prototype is built [2].

knowledge_max_2: Computer software is used to design products
Designs can be created, modified and tested digitally before manufacture

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halyard Lighting of using CAD in its design work.
questions.model_answer: First, design speed improved [k]; revisions that once took 3 weeks can now be completed in 4 days [app]. Second, material waste fell [k]; prototyping waste dropped by 40% because errors are spotted on screen [app].

knowledge_max_2: Faster design and revision process
Reduced waste and errors before prototyping
application_max_2: Revisions completed in 4 days instead of 3 weeks
Prototyping waste fell by 40%

questions.question_text: Explain two costs or drawbacks of CAD for Halyard Lighting Co.
questions.model_answer: First, ongoing licence costs [k]: the software licence is due for renewal at $18,000 per year [app], so the $95,000 purchase is not a one-off cost and profits will be reduced every year [an]. Second, dependence on skilled staff [k]: two senior designers on $42,000 salaries were hired to run it [app], so the business faces retraining costs and disruption if they leave or the software is replaced [an].

knowledge_max_2: High purchase and recurring licence/maintenance costs
Need for trained specialist staff and risk of dependency

Two senior designers hired on $42,000 salaries to run it

questions.question_text: Do you think Halyard Lighting Co should buy 2 more CAD licences instead of hiring another designer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, more licences extend a proven advantage [k]; CAD already cut design revisions from 3 weeks to 4 days and prototyping waste by 40% [app]; giving the existing design team of 6 more licences would let everyone work simultaneously, cutting revision queues and supporting the $2.1 million sales pipeline [an]. However, licences alone cannot originate ideas [k]; the licence costs $18,000 per year on top of $95,000 already spent, and two senior designers already earn $42,000 salaries [app]; another designer would add fresh creative capacity, share the workload at peaks and reduce over-reliance on the software [an]. Overall I recommend buying the 2 licences first, because the 4-day revision turnaround and 40% waste saving show CAD is delivering value [eval]; if design orders keep growing, hire a designer later rather than carry both costs at once [eval].

A new designer adds creative capacity and reduces dependence on licences/software

scenario_stem:
Dunmere Plastics Ltd is an injection-moulding business in Country X producing plastic housings for washing machines, lawnmowers and dishwashers, trading for 8 years. The factory runs two 8-hour shifts, five days a week. It recently installed CAM software costing $320,000 to control its 8 moulding machines directly from programs written by the production office. CAM programs also log every machine fault automatically.

Machine set-up time has fallen from 45 minutes to 12 minutes, and scrap has fallen from 9% to 4% of output. Annual output is now 950,000 housings, exported to 3 countries. Orders from 2 washing-machine plants account for 80% of output. The managing director is considering extending CAM to the final assembly robot, which would displace 12 of the 120 employees.

questions.question_text: Define 'CAM (computer-aided manufacturing)'.
questions.model_answer: CAM is the use of computer software to control machines and manufacturing processes directly during production [2].

knowledge_max_2: Computer software controls machines/processes
Used to plan and run manufacturing directly in production

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of CAM for Dunmere Plastics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, faster set-ups [k]; machine set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes [app]. Second, less waste [k]; scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reduced machine set-up/changeover time
Reduced scrap/waste and errors
application_max_2: Set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes
Scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunmere Plastics may face if it extends CAM to the final assembly robot.
questions.model_answer: First, job losses and morale [k]: extending CAM to assembly would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app], which could damage motivation, raise turnover and harm the business's reputation as an employer [an]. Second, high extra cost and risk [k]: after spending $320,000 on moulding CAM, another system must be bought and integrated [app], so if exports to the 3 countries slow, the investment may take longer to repay and strain cash flow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Redundancies/job losses harming morale and reputation
High additional capital cost and repayment risk

$320,000 already spent on the moulding CAM system
analysis_max_2: Displaced workers may leave, reducing goodwill and raising training costs for remaining staff

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunmere Plastics should extend CAM to the final assembly robot? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, assembly CAM would compound the gains [k]; moulding CAM already cut set-ups from 45 to 12 minutes and scrap from 9% to 4%, with 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries [app]; extending computer control to assembly could deliver the same consistency at the final stage and help win larger export contracts [an]. However, assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app]; the moulding system already cost $320,000 [k], and forcing 12 redundancies could lower morale, raise absenteeism and increase long-run labour costs among those remaining [an]. Overall I recommend extending CAM to assembly only if the 12 affected workers are retrained or redeployed [eval]; the quality and export benefits justify the move, but rushing it without reskilling would risk the workforce goodwill the business still needs [eval].

scenario_stem:
Aldercroft Auto Components is a private limited company in Country X producing suspension brackets and exhaust flanges for 2 car assembly plants. It employs 240 workers at a single factory on an industrial estate. Two years ago the business invested $1.2 million in a CIM system linking its design office, 14 CNC machines, quality scanners and a stock control database.

The system passes CAD designs straight to CAM files, schedules machine use automatically and flags defects on the line. Defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5%, and average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock. However, CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries, and the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan.

questions.question_text: Define 'CIM (computer-integrated manufacturing)'.
questions.model_answer: CIM is the use of a single computer system to link and control all stages of production, from design through manufacture to quality and stock control [2].

Covers design, manufacture, quality and stock/inventory control in one integrated system

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
questions.model_answer: First, better product quality [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% after the system was installed [app]. Second, faster delivery [k]; average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: Improved quality/fewer defects
Faster lead time/quicker deliveries
application_max_2: Defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5%
Average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days

questions.question_text: Explain two risks or costs of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
questions.model_answer: First, dependence on specialist staff [k]: CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app], so if they leave, the whole production line could stall until replacements are found and trained [an]. Second, financial risk [k]: the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan [app], so the business must keep the 2 assembly plants' orders profitable enough to meet interest payments, or face cash-flow pressure if orders fall [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on scarce specialist IT staff
High capital cost financed by borrowing

$1.2 million financed by a bank loan

questions.model_answer: Yes, rolling CIM out to a second hall would replicate proven gains [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% and lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days [app]; a second hall could cut buffer stocks for both assembly plants, win more orders and spread the fixed costs of the CIM system [an]. However, the first $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan and the system already needs 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app]; duplicating it doubles loan pressure, and one technical failure could halt even more limited IT capacity [an], even though integration usually lifts productivity [k]. Overall I recommend a phased second-hall rollout funded from operating surplus rather than new borrowing [eval], because the 4.5-point defect fall and 12-day lead-time cut are compelling, but only once the 2 technicians confirm the system is stable [eval].

scenario_stem:
Dorchester Village Stores operates 6 grocery supermarkets in Country X, employing 145 staff. Last year it spent $180,000 installing EPOS tills in all 6 stores. Each checkout now scans barcodes, records sales by the hour and updates a central stock database automatically. The head office believes EPOS will free staff from manual stock counts.

EPOS data shows fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months. The system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales. Trading on a Saturday can reach $38,000 per store, so managers worry automatic orders may over-buy perishables before quiet weekdays. The board is debating whether EPOS should place automatic reorders or whether store managers should approve all orders above $5,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'EPOS (electronic point of sale)'.
questions.model_answer: EPOS is a computerised checkout system that records sales and stock information electronically when goods are scanned at the till [2].

knowledge_max_2: Computerised checkout/till system
Records sales and stock data electronically at point of sale

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of EPOS for Dorchester Village Stores.
questions.model_answer: First, reduced wastage [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months [app]. Second, better reordering [k]; the system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower wastage/better stock control
Automatic reordering and sales data capture
application_max_2: Fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% within 4 months
EPOS flags product lines below 2 weeks of expected sales

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dorchester Village Stores holds inventories.
questions.model_answer: First, to meet customer demand without running out [k]; EPOS flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales [app], so holding enough stock prevents lost sales and protects customer loyalty on busy Saturdays [an]. Second, to balance wastage against availability [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% after EPOS began tracking sales [app], showing that accurate stock data lets the business hold the right amount instead of over-ordering perishables [an].

knowledge_max_2: Meets customer demand and avoids stockouts
Supports efficient purchasing and reduces waste
application_max_2: EPOS flags product lines below 2 weeks of expected sales
Fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% within 4 months
analysis_max_2: Avoiding stockouts prevents lost sales and supports customer loyalty, especially on Saturdays
Accurate sales data reduces over-ordering of perishables, cutting waste and improving profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Dorchester Village Stores should let EPOS place automatic reorders rather than keep manual approval? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, automatic reorders match stock to real demand [k]; EPOS already cut fresh-food wastage from 12% to 7% and records sales hourly [app]; automatic replenishment of the 400 key lines below 2 weeks of expected sales would prevent stockouts on busy Saturdays, when each store can take $38,000 [an]. However, managers fear over-ordering perishables [k]; the board is split on whether orders above $5,000 need manual sign-off [app], and a system error could multiply across 6 stores before anyone notices, wasting cash and shelf space [an]. Overall I recommend automatic reorders for dry goods, keeping manual approval only above $5,000 for fresh lines [eval]; this captures most efficiency gains while protecting cash where wastage is most costly [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automatic ordering links stock to real-time demand
Manual checks reduce risk of over-ordering and system errors
application_max_2: EPOS cut wastage from 12% to 7% and flags 400 key lines below 2 weeks of expected sales
Debate over whether orders above $5,000 need manual sign-off; Saturday trading can reach $38,000 per store
analysis_max_2: Automatic reordering prevents lost sales and frees staff from manual stock counts

evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation

scenario_stem:
Tannersley Glassworks is a glass bottle manufacturer in Country X that has supplied soft-drink bottlers for 16 years. Its 120 workers produced 240,000 bottles per week, an average of 2,000 bottles per worker per week. After installing 2 new furnaces and an extra forming machine costing $900,000, the factory made 288,000 bottles per week with 96 workers. The factory operates three shifts, six days a week.

That equals 3,000 bottles per worker per week, a 50% rise in productivity, and annual output is now about 15 million bottles, up from 12.5 million. The $900,000 was borrowed from a bank. Overtime would cost $16 per hour time-and-a-half, while a furnace would take 18 months to install but last 25 years. Bottlers want an extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract.

questions.question_text: Define 'productivity'.
questions.model_answer: Productivity is the output produced per worker, or per other input, over a given time period [2].

knowledge_max_2: Output per worker/per input
Measured over a period of time

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between production and productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, what they measure [k]; production is total output, which rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week, while productivity is output per worker, which rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker [app]. Second, how each is increased [k]; production can be raised by adding workers or overtime, while productivity rose because 96 workers replaced 120 after the new machines arrived [app].

knowledge_max_2: Production = total output; productivity = output per worker/per input
Production can be raised by more inputs; productivity by more efficient use of inputs
application_max_2: Total output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week
Output per worker rose from 2,000 to 3,000 after the workforce fell from 120 to 96

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tannersley Glassworks of the rise in productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, lower labour cost per bottle [k]; output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while the workforce fell from 120 to 96 [app], so fixed costs are spread over more units and the business can improve profit to help repay the $900,000 loan [an]. Second, stronger competitiveness [k]; each of the 96 remaining workers now produces 3,000 bottles per week [app], so unit costs fall and Tannersley can undercut rivals to win the contract for an extra 40,000 bottles a week [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher output per worker lowers average cost per unit
Improved efficiency and competitiveness
application_max_2: Output rose 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while staff fell from 120 to 96
Each worker now produces 3,000 bottles per week
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs are spread over more bottles, improving profit and ability to repay the bank loan
Lower unit costs strengthen competitiveness and support winning the extra 40,000 bottles contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Tannersley Glassworks should raise output further by overtime or by buying a third furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, a third furnace would replicate the gains [k]; productivity already rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after the 2 new furnaces were installed [app]; a third furnace would last 25 years and help supply bottlers the extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract [an]. However, overtime is more flexible right now [k]; the $900,000 was borrowed and overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half adds capacity without new long-term debt [app]; but overtime raises labour cost per bottle and cannot match machine efficiency or consistent quality [an]. Overall I recommend buying the third furnace, financed partly from retained profit, because the proven 50% productivity rise shows machines outperform overtime [eval]; if demand softens before contracts are signed, delay the furnace and use overtime as a stop-gap [eval].

Overtime adds capacity quickly but at higher unit cost
application_max_2: Productivity rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after 2 new furnaces
$900,000 loan outstanding; overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half; furnace would take 18 months and last 25 years
analysis_max_2: A third furnace locks in capacity and consistency to fulfil the 40,000 bottles weekly contract
Overtime protects cash flow now but erodes unit economics and quality consistency

scenario_stem:
Dunnock Cheese Co is a private limited company in Country X making cheddar from milk supplied by 26 local farms. Sales are made to supermarkets across the northern region. It employs 40 workers and runs 3 pasteurising vats in a converted barn on the edge of the market town. Each month it produces 18,000 kg of cheese from 180,000 litres of milk bought at $0.42 per litre.

Monthly revenue is $198,000 against production costs of $171,000, leaving a profit of $27,000. The company currently turns down orders worth $9,000 a month because the vats are fully booked. The directors are considering a fourth vat costing $150,000 to raise capacity by 25%, but supplies of raw milk and skilled cheesemakers are both limited locally.

Second, secure more inputs [k]; buying more milk from the 26 local farms or signing new suppliers would let the 3 existing vats run closer to full capacity [app].

knowledge_max_2: Increase capacity/capital equipment
Secure more inputs (raw materials, labour) or use existing capacity fully
application_max_2: Fourth vat costing $150,000 would raise capacity by 25% (18,000 kg to 22,500 kg)

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Dunnock Cheese Co could use its resources more effectively.
questions.model_answer: First, reduce milk waste and improve yields [k]; each month 180,000 litres of milk are bought at $0.42 per litre [app], so better pasteurising yields would cut the $75,600 monthly milk bill or raise output of 18,000 kg [an]. Second, plan labour and vats better [k]; with 40 workers and full order books [app], scheduling vat runs around milk deliveries could lift output without the $150,000 vat purchase [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing waste/improving input efficiency
Better planning and scheduling of labour and capital
application_max_2: 180,000 litres of milk bought at $0.42 per litre each month
40 workers and 3 vats in use; orders worth $9,000 a month turned away
analysis_max_2: Better yields spread the milk cost over more cheese, raising profit per kg
Smarter scheduling raises output without new capital spending, easing pressure on the $150,000 decision

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunnock Cheese Co should buy the fourth vat now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, the fourth vat would capture lost sales [k]; the vats are fully booked and the business turns down orders worth $9,000 a month [app]; a 25% capacity increase to 22,500 kg would lift revenue above $198,000 and push profit beyond $27,000 [an]. However, milk and cheesemaker supplies are limited [k]; the 26 local farms already supply 180,000 litres a month, and hiring skilled cheesemakers locally is hard [app]; spending $150,000 without guaranteed inputs could leave an expensive vat idle and strain cash [an]. Overall I recommend buying the fourth vat only after securing extra milk contracts and at least one cheesemaker [eval]; demand clearly exists, but the vat will not pay for itself if inputs stay capped [eval].

scenario_stem:
Montclair Electronics Plc is a public limited company in Country X manufacturing printed circuit boards for washing machines and televisions. The company sells to appliance makers in 5 countries and exports 70% of output. In 2024 it invested $2.6 million in surface-mount placement machines and automated inspection equipment, moving 60% of assembly from hand soldering to automation.

Monthly output rose from 90,000 to 130,000 boards and the defect rate fell from 5% to 0.8%. The changes made 150 of the 400 hand-soldering jobs redundant at a cost of $1.9 million. Remaining workers now tend placement machines and earn $14 per hour. The board sees final testing as the last manual bottleneck and debates automating it; the testing line employs 48 workers.

scenario_stem:
Quillbrook Pens Ltd is a small manufacturer in Country X producing luxury brass fountain pens, employing 28 workers. Pens retail at $180 each and are popular with corporate gift buyers. Designs are drawn using CAD and batches of 500 pens are made to order before the November gift season. The business holds 3 months of raw materials — brass rods, ink and polished barrels — at a storage cost of $7,500 per month. Storage space is limited to 900 square metres.

EPOS sales data from 40 stockist shops shows demand spikes sharply in November, so running out of stock in October would lose the season's sales. The directors are debating whether to build inventory to 4 months' supply or arrange faster deliveries from the brass supplier.

Keep production running between deliveries

Second, cash tied up [k]: money spent on raw materials cannot be used elsewhere [app], and if November demand disappoints, the excess stock of polished barrels and ink may never be used, risking obsolescence [an].
